assessment.nobel_worthiness: Targeted protein degradation reframed drug discovery: small molecules that recruit E3 ligases to destroy rather than inhibit a target (PROTAC concept, cereblon as the thalidomide target underlying molecular glues). A clear conceptual invention with a rapidly growing clinical pipeline, and a chemical idea that is easy to state.
assessment.attribution: Crews and Deshaies conceived and first demonstrated heterobifunctional degraders; Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide-binding protein that explains glue degraders. Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and others made major later contributions, so a three-person split is a judgement call; the glue and PROTAC strands may deserve different weight.
assessment.maturity: Early proof-of-concept is decades old and has been independently reproduced widely, but clinical validation is still maturing (few approved degraders). Timing is plausible rather than overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should centre on PROTACs, on molecular glues, or both, and how to weigh Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto.
Clinical benefit is not yet settled at scale.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (1985) made ab initio dynamics of condensed matter routine by unifying electronic-structure and nuclear motion. Foundational, original, with a vast and durable impact across chemistry, materials and physics.
assessment.attribution: The credit is unusually clean: a single 1985 paper by two authors. Parrinello also appears on other candidates (metadynamics, machine-learned potentials), which could complicate how credit is allocated across a single prize.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of independent use and confirmation; fully mature and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Overlap of Parrinello with metadynamics and machine-learned potential candidates.
Whether the committee views this as chemistry or as physics-of-materials methodology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reading single DNA or RNA molecules electrically through a nanopore is a nanoscale-physics idea that became a commercial sequencing technology with long-read capability. Original, concrete, and impactful in genomics and analytical chemistry.
assessment.attribution: Deamer, Branton and Kasianowicz launched the concept (1996); Akeson demonstrated polymer reading and enzyme-controlled translocation; Bayley engineered protein pores and drove the Oxford Nanopore route. Branton's role is substantial, but I am not certain of the current status of all credited individuals and cannot select names outside the list; the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Technology is well established and independently validated, with wide field adoption; recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Akeson and Bayley is unresolved, and I am not certain which are living.
Fit to chemistry versus physics or technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Halide perovskites transformed photovoltaics: efficiencies rose from a few percent to above 25 percent within about a decade, with a deep physics-chemistry puzzle in defect tolerance. Very high impact and originality.
assessment.attribution: Miyasaka reported the first perovskite-sensitised cell (2009); Park delivered the solid-state 2012 device; Snaith showed the thin-film, meso-superstructured and planar variants. Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis are also strongly credited, so the three-person cut is contentious.
assessment.maturity: Efficiency is independently confirmed, but long-term stability, lead toxicity and commercial viability remain open, so the case may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Operational stability not yet proven at scale.
Contentious allocation among six credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Biomolecular condensates formed by liquid-liquid phase separation changed how cellular organisation is understood and brought polymer physics into cell biology. Conceptually original, very broad influence, and good physical-chemistry content.
assessment.attribution: Brangwynne and Hyman's 2009 P-granule work launched the field; Rosen's multivalent-interaction model provided the physical-chemical basis. Pappu and Mittag contributed key theory and sequence-grammar work.
assessment.maturity: Concept is confirmed by many labs, but functional significance in vivo is still debated, with questions about what counts as true phase separation. A little early.
uncertainties: Physiological relevance versus in vitro demonstration remains debated.
Whether chemistry or biology/medicine is the better home.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resolving the internal bond structure of single molecules with CO-functionalised noncontact AFM gave a direct image of chemical structure and bond order, with applications to on-surface synthesis and reaction products. Clear, striking and technically original; Giessibl's qPlus sensor was the enabling technology.
assessment.attribution: Gross, Meyer and colleagues at IBM Zurich produced the 2009 landmark; Giessibl developed the qPlus sensor. Eigler and Ho are credited for related single-atom/molecule manipulation and spectroscopy, which is a different strand. Three names fit best.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced across groups; established. Impact on mainstream chemistry is narrower than on surface science.
uncertainties: Narrower community and application breadth than other candidates.
Separating the imaging strand from the manipulation strand.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single-molecule FRET opened direct observation of conformational dynamics and heterogeneity in biomolecules, a widely used physical-chemistry method that links optics with chemical mechanism.
assessment.attribution: Weiss and Ha established the early solution and surface measurements (1996); Zhuang applied it to RNA catalysis and developed related methods; Selvin contributed the in vitro motor-tracking strand. Credit is plausible but spread across several people.
assessment.maturity: Mature and standard in the field; however, recognition of single-molecule methods overlaps with the 2014 super-resolution prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior recognition of single-molecule and super-resolution work.
Allocation of credit among four names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: DNA origami and programmable DNA nanostructures showed that nucleic acids can be folded and assembled into arbitrary nanoscale shapes. Highly original, with broad nanotechnology reach, though real-world chemical impact is still developing.
assessment.attribution: Rothemund's 2006 origami paper is the decisive step; Winfree developed algorithmic self-assembly and Yan's group made structural 2D/3D constructs. Seeman's foundational role is outside the supplied credited names, which complicates fairness.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely used, but the applications are still emerging; the prize may be early.
uncertainties: Absence of the field's founder from the credited names.
Practical impact beyond research tools is limited so far.
